analysis-i: The files in this directory contain a formalization of my text [_Analysis I_](https://terrytao.wordpress.com/books/analysis-i/) into [Lean](https://lean-lang.org/). The formalization is intended to be as faithful a paraphrasing as possible to the original text, while also showcasing Lean's features and syntax.  In particular, the formalization is _not_ optimized for efficiency, and in some cases may deviate from idiomatic Lean usage.

Portions of the text that were left as exercises to the reader are rendered in this translation as `sorry`s.  Readers are welcome to fork the repository here to try their hand at these exercises, but I do not intend to place solutions in this repository directly.

While the arrangement of definitions, theorems, and proofs here are closely paraphrasing the textbook, I am refraining from directly quoting material from the textbook, instead providing references to the original text where appropriate.  As such, this formalization should be viewed as an annotated companion to the primary text, rather than a replacement for it.

Much of the material in this text is duplicated in Lean's standard math library [Mathlib](https://leanprover-community.github.io/mathlib4_docs/), though with slightly different definitions.  To reconcile these discrepancies, this formalization will gradually transition from the textbook-provided definitions to the Mathlib-provided definitions as one progresses further into the text, thus sacrificing the self-containedness of the formalization in favor of compatibility with Mathlib.  For instance, Chapter 2 develops a theory of the natural numbers independent of Mathlib, but all subsequent chapters will use the Mathlib natural numbers instead.  (An epilogue to Chapter 2 is provided to show that the two notions of the natural numbers are isomorphic.)  As such, this formalization can also be used as an introduction to various portions of Mathlib.
In order to align the formalization with Mathlib conventions, a small number of technical changes have been made to some of the definitions as compared with the textbook version.  Most notably:

- Sequences are indexed to start from zero rather than from one, as Mathlib has much more support for the 0-based natural numbers `ℕ` than the 1-based natural numbers.
- Many operations that are left undefined in the text, such as division by zero, or taking the formal limit of a non-Cauchy sequence, are instead assigned a "junk" value (e.g., `0`) to make the operation totally defined.  This is because Lean has better support for total functions than partial functions (indiscriminate use of the latter can lead into "dependent type hell" in which even very basic manipulations require quite subtle and delicate proofs).  See for instance [this blog post](https://xenaproject.wordpress.com/2020/07/05/division-by-zero-in-type-theory-a-faq/) by Kevin Buzzard for more discussion.
- The Chapter 2 natural numbers are constructed by an inductive type, rather than via a purely axiomatic approach.  However, the Peano Axioms are formalized in [the epilogue to this chapter](https://teorth.github.io/analysis/Analysis/Section_2_epilogue/).

sections.title: Section 2.1: The Peano Axioms
sections.doc:
This file is a translation of Section 2.1 of Analysis I to Lean 4.  All numbering refers to the
original text.

I have attempted to make the translation as faithful a paraphrasing as possible of the original
text.  When there is a choice between a more idiomatic Lean solution and a more faithful
translation, I have generally chosen the latter.  In particular, there will be places where the
Lean code could be "golfed" to be more elegant and idiomatic, but I have consciously avoided doing
so.

Main constructions and results of this section:

- Definition of the "Chapter 2" natural numbers, `Chapter2.Nat`,abbreviated as {name}`Nat` within
  the Chapter2 namespace. (In the book, the natural numbers are treated in a purely axiomatic
  fashion, as a type that obeys the Peano axioms; but here we take advantage of Lean's native
  inductive types to explicitly construct a version of the natural numbers that obey those axioms.
  One could also proceed more axiomatically, as is done in Section 3 for set theory: see the
  epilogue to this chapter.)
- Establishment of the Peano axioms for `Chapter2.Nat`.
- Recursive definitions for `Chapter2.Nat`.

Note: at the end of this chapter, the `Chapter2.Nat` class will be deprecated in favor of the
standard Mathlib class {name}`_root_.Nat`, or {lean}`ℕ`.  However, we will develop the properties of
`Chapter2.Nat` "by hand" in the next few sections for pedagogical purposes.

declarations.name: Chapter2.Nat
declarations.doc:
Assumption 2.6 (Existence of natural numbers). Here we use an explicit construction of the
natural numbers (using an inductive type). For a more axiomatic approach, see the epilogue to
this chapter.
declarations.statement: inductive Nat

declarations.name: Chapter2.Nat.instZero
declarations.statement: instance Nat.instZero : Zero Nat

declarations.name: Chapter2.Nat.instOfNat
declarations.doc:
Definition 2.1.3 (Definition of the numerals 0, 1, 2, etc.). Note: to avoid ambiguity, one may
need to use explicit casts such as {lean}`(0:Nat)`, {lean}`(1:Nat)`, etc. to refer to this
chapter's version of the natural numbers.
declarations.statement: instance Nat.instOfNat {n:_root_.Nat} : OfNat Nat n

declarations.name: Chapter2.Nat.two_succ
declarations.statement: lemma Nat.two_succ : 2++ = 3

declarations.name: Chapter2.Nat.succ_ne
declarations.doc:
Axiom 2.3 (0 is not the successor of any natural number).
Compare with Lean's {name}`Nat.succ_ne_zero`.
declarations.statement: theorem Nat.succ_ne (n:Nat) : n++ ≠ 0

declarations.name: Chapter2.Nat.four_ne
declarations.doc: Proposition 2.1.6 (4 is not equal to zero)
declarations.statement: theorem Nat.four_ne : (4:Nat) ≠ 0

declarations.name: Chapter2.Nat.succ_cancel
declarations.doc:
Axiom 2.4 (Different natural numbers have different successors).
Compare with Mathlib's {name}`Nat.succ_inj`.
declarations.statement: theorem Nat.succ_cancel {n m:Nat} (hnm: n++ = m++) : n = m

declarations.name: Chapter2.Nat.succ_ne_succ
declarations.doc:
Axiom 2.4 (Different natural numbers have different successors).
Compare with Mathlib's {name}`Nat.succ_ne_succ`.
declarations.statement: theorem Nat.succ_ne_succ (n m:Nat) : n ≠ m → n++ ≠ m++

declarations.name: Chapter2.Nat.six_ne_two
declarations.statement: theorem Nat.six_ne_two : (6:Nat) ≠ 2

declarations.name: Chapter2.Nat.induction
declarations.doc:
Axiom 2.5 (Principle of mathematical induction). The {tactic}`induction` (or
{tactic}`induction'`) tactic in Mathlib serves as a substitute for this axiom.
declarations.statement:
theorem Nat.induction (P : Nat → Prop) (hbase : P 0) (hind : ∀ n, P n → P (n++)) :
    ∀ n, P n

declarations.name: Chapter2.Nat.recurse_zero
declarations.statement: theorem Nat.recurse_zero (f: Nat → Nat → Nat) (c: Nat) : Nat.recurse f c 0 = c

declarations.name: Chapter2.Nat.recurse_succ
declarations.statement:
theorem Nat.recurse_succ (f: Nat → Nat → Nat) (c: Nat) (n: Nat) :
    recurse f c (n++) = f n (recurse f c n)

declarations.name: Chapter2.Nat.eq_recurse
declarations.statement:
theorem Nat.eq_recurse (f: Nat → Nat → Nat) (c: Nat) (a: Nat → Nat) :
    (a 0 = c ∧ ∀ n, a (n++) = f n (a n)) ↔ a = recurse f c

declarations.name: Chapter2.Nat.recurse_uniq
declarations.statement:
theorem Nat.recurse_uniq (f: Nat → Nat → Nat) (c: Nat) :
    ∃! (a: Nat → Nat), a 0 = c ∧ ∀ n, a (n++) = f n (a n)

sections.title: Section 2.2: Addition
sections.doc:
This file is a translation of Section 2.2 of Analysis I to Lean 4.  All numbering refers to the
original text.

I have attempted to make the translation as faithful a paraphrasing as possible of the original
text. When there is a choice between a more idiomatic Lean solution and a more faithful
translation, I have generally chosen the latter.  In particular, there will be places where the
Lean code could be "golfed" to be more elegant and idiomatic, but I have consciously avoided
doing so.

Main constructions and results of this section:

- Definition of addition and order for the "Chapter 2" natural numbers, {name}`Chapter2.Nat`.
- Establishment of basic properties of addition and order.

Note: at the end of this chapter, the {name}`Chapter2.Nat` class will be deprecated in favor of the
standard Mathlib class {name}`_root_.Nat`, or {lean}`ℕ`.  However, we will develop the properties of
{name}`Chapter2.Nat` "by hand" for pedagogical purposes.

## Tips from past users

Users of the companion who have completed the exercises in this section are welcome to send their
tips for future users in this section as PRs.

- (Add tip here)

declarations.name: Chapter2.Nat.add
declarations.doc:
Definition 2.2.1. (Addition of natural numbers).
Compare with Mathlib's {name}`Nat.add`
declarations.statement: abbrev Nat.add (n m : Nat) : Nat

declarations.name: Chapter2.Nat.add_zero
declarations.statement: lemma Nat.add_zero (n:Nat) : n + 0 = n

declarations.name: Chapter2.Nat.add_succ
declarations.statement: lemma Nat.add_succ (n m:Nat) : n + (m++) = (n + m)++

declarations.name: Chapter2.Nat.add_comm
declarations.doc: Proposition 2.2.4 (Addition is commutative). Compare with Mathlib's {name}`Nat.add_comm`
declarations.statement: theorem Nat.add_comm (n m:Nat) : n + m = m + n

declarations.name: Chapter2.Nat.add_assoc
declarations.doc:
Proposition 2.2.5 (Addition is associative) / Exercise 2.2.1
Compare with Mathlib's {name}`Nat.add_assoc`.
declarations.statement: theorem Nat.add_assoc (a b c:Nat) : (a + b) + c = a + (b + c)

declarations.name: Chapter2.Nat.add_left_cancel
declarations.statement: theorem Nat.add_left_cancel (a b c:Nat) (habc: a + b = a + c) : b = c

declarations.name: Chapter2.Nat.IsPos
declarations.statement: def Nat.IsPos (n:Nat) : Prop

declarations.name: Chapter2.Nat.add_pos_left
declarations.doc:
Proposition 2.2.8 (positive plus natural number is positive).
Compare with Mathlib's {name}`Nat.add_pos_left`.
declarations.statement: theorem Nat.add_pos_left {a:Nat} (b:Nat) (ha: a.IsPos) : (a + b).IsPos

declarations.name: Chapter2.Nat.add_eq_zero
declarations.doc:
Corollary 2.2.9 (if sum vanishes, then summands vanish).
Compare with Mathlib's {name}`Nat.add_eq_zero`.
declarations.statement: theorem Nat.add_eq_zero (a b:Nat) (hab: a + b = 0) : a = 0 ∧ b = 0

declarations.name: Chapter2.Nat.uniq_succ_eq
declarations.statement: lemma Nat.uniq_succ_eq (a:Nat) (ha: a.IsPos) : ∃! b, b++ = a

declarations.name: Chapter2.Nat.instLE
declarations.doc:
Definition 2.2.11 (Ordering of the natural numbers).
This defines the {kw (of := «term_≤_»)}`≤` notation on the natural numbers.
declarations.statement: instance Nat.instLE : LE Nat

declarations.name: Chapter2.Nat.instLT
declarations.doc:
Definition 2.2.11 (Ordering of the natural numbers).
This defines the {kw (of := «term_<_»)}`<` notation on the natural numbers.
declarations.statement: instance Nat.instLT : LT Nat

declarations.name: Chapter2.Nat.ge_refl
declarations.doc:
Proposition 2.2.12 (Basic properties of order for natural numbers) / Exercise 2.2.3

(a) (Order is reflexive). Compare with Mathlib's {name}`Nat.le_refl`.
declarations.statement: theorem Nat.ge_refl (a:Nat) : a ≥ a

declarations.name: Chapter2.Nat.trichotomous
declarations.doc:
Proposition 2.2.13 (Trichotomy of order for natural numbers) / Exercise 2.2.4
Compare with Mathlib's {name}`trichotomous`.  Parts of this theorem have been placed
in the preceding Lean theorems.
declarations.statement: theorem Nat.trichotomous (a b:Nat) : a < b ∨ a = b ∨ a > b

declarations.name: Chapter2.Nat.strong_induction
declarations.doc:
Proposition 2.2.14 (Strong principle of induction) / Exercise 2.2.5
Compare with Mathlib's {name}`Nat.strong_induction_on`.

declarations.name: Chapter2.Nat.backwards_induction
Chapter2.Nat.induction_from
declarations.doc:
Exercise 2.2.7 (induction from a starting point)
Compare with Mathlib's {name}`Nat.le_induction`.
declarations.statement:
theorem Nat.induction_from {n:Nat} {P: Nat → Prop} (hind: ∀ m, P m → P (m++)) :
    P n → ∀ m, m ≥ n → P m

sections.title: Section 2.3: Multiplication
sections.doc:
This file is a translation of Section 2.3 of Analysis I to Lean 4. All numbering refers to the
original text.

I have attempted to make the translation as faithful a paraphrasing as possible of the original
text. When there is a choice between a more idiomatic Lean solution and a more faithful
translation, I have generally chosen the latter.  In particular, there will be places where the
Lean code could be "golfed" to be more elegant and idiomatic, but I have consciously avoided
doing so.

Main constructions and results of this section:

- Definition of multiplication and exponentiation for the "Chapter 2" natural numbers,
  {name}`Chapter2.Nat`.

Note: at the end of this chapter, the {name}`Chapter2.Nat` class will be deprecated in favor of the
standard Mathlib class {name}`_root_.Nat`, or {lean}`ℕ`.  However, we will develop the properties of
{name}`Chapter2.Nat` "by hand" for pedagogical purposes.

## Tips from past users

Users of the companion who have completed the exercises in this section are welcome to send their tips for future users in this section as PRs.

declarations.statement: abbrev Nat.mul (n m : Nat) : Nat

declarations.doc:
Definition 2.3.1 (Multiplication of natural numbers)
Compare with Mathlib's {name}`Nat.zero_mul`
declarations.statement: theorem Nat.zero_mul (m: Nat) : 0 * m = 0

declarations.name: Chapter2.Nat.succ_mul
declarations.doc:
Definition 2.3.1 (Multiplication of natural numbers)
Compare with Mathlib's {name}`Nat.succ_mul`
declarations.statement: theorem Nat.succ_mul (n m: Nat) : (n++) * m = n * m + m

declarations.name: Chapter2.Nat.mul_comm
declarations.doc:
Lemma 2.3.2 (Multiplication is commutative) / Exercise 2.3.1
Compare with Mathlib's {name}`Nat.mul_comm`
declarations.statement: lemma Nat.mul_comm (n m: Nat) : n * m = m * n

declarations.name: Chapter2.Nat.mul_eq_zero
declarations.doc:
Lemma 2.3.3 (Positive natural numbers have no zero divisors) / Exercise 2.3.2.
Compare with Mathlib's {name}`Nat.mul_eq_zero`.

declarations.name: Chapter2.Nat.mul_add
declarations.statement: theorem Nat.mul_add (a b c: Nat) : a * (b + c) = a * b + a * c

declarations.name: Chapter2.Nat.add_mul
declarations.statement: theorem Nat.add_mul (a b c: Nat) : (a + b)*c = a*c + b*c

declarations.name: Chapter2.Nat.mul_assoc

Proposition 2.3.5 (Multiplication is associative) / Exercise 2.3.3
Compare with Mathlib's {name}`Nat.mul_assoc`
declarations.statement: theorem Nat.mul_assoc (a b c: Nat) : (a * b) * c = a * (b * c)

declarations.name: Chapter2.Nat.mul_lt_mul_of_pos_right

Proposition 2.3.6 (Multiplication preserves order)
Compare with Mathlib's {name}`Nat.mul_lt_mul_of_pos_right`
declarations.statement: theorem Nat.mul_lt_mul_of_pos_right {a b c: Nat} (h: a < b) (hc: c.IsPos) : a * c < b * c

declarations.name: Chapter2.Nat.mul_gt_mul_of_pos_right
declarations.statement:
theorem Nat.mul_gt_mul_of_pos_right {a b c: Nat} (h: a > b) (hc: c.IsPos) :
    a * c > b * c

declarations.name: Chapter2.Nat.mul_lt_mul_of_pos_left
declarations.doc:
Proposition 2.3.6 (Multiplication preserves order)
Compare with Mathlib's {name}`Nat.mul_lt_mul_of_pos_left`
declarations.statement: theorem Nat.mul_lt_mul_of_pos_left {a b c: Nat} (h: a < b) (hc: c.IsPos) : c * a < c * b

declarations.name: Chapter2.Nat.mul_gt_mul_of_pos_left
declarations.statement:
theorem Nat.mul_gt_mul_of_pos_left {a b c: Nat} (h: a > b) (hc: c.IsPos) :
    c * a > c * b

declarations.name: Chapter2.Nat.mul_cancel_right
declarations.statement: lemma Nat.mul_cancel_right {a b c: Nat} (h: a * c = b * c) (hc: c.IsPos) : a = b

declarations.name: Chapter2.Nat.exists_div_mod
declarations.doc:
Proposition 2.3.9 (Euclid's division lemma) / Exercise 2.3.5
Compare with Mathlib's {name}`Nat.mod_eq_iff`
declarations.statement:
theorem Nat.exists_div_mod (n:Nat) {q: Nat} (hq: q.IsPos) :
    ∃ m r: Nat, 0 ≤ r ∧ r < q ∧ n = m * q + r

declarations.name: Chapter2.Nat.pow
declarations.statement: abbrev Nat.pow (m n: Nat) : Nat

declarations.name: Chapter2.Nat.pow_zero
declarations.doc:
Definition 2.3.11 (Exponentiation for natural numbers)
Compare with Mathlib's {name}`Nat.pow_zero`
declarations.statement: theorem Nat.pow_zero (m: Nat) : m ^ (0:Nat) = 1

declarations.name: Chapter2.Nat.zero_pow_zero
declarations.statement: theorem Nat.zero_pow_zero : (0:Nat) ^ 0 = 1

declarations.name: Chapter2.Nat.pow_succ
declarations.doc:
Definition 2.3.11 (Exponentiation for natural numbers)
Compare with Mathlib's {name}`Nat.pow_succ`
declarations.statement: theorem Nat.pow_succ (m n: Nat) : (m:Nat) ^ n++ = m^n * m

declarations.name: Chapter2.Nat.sq_add_eq
declarations.statement:
theorem Nat.sq_add_eq (a b: Nat) :
    (a + b) ^ (2 : Nat) = a ^ (2 : Nat) + 2 * a * b + b ^ (2 : Nat)

sections.title: Chapter 2 epilogue: Isomorphism with the Mathlib natural numbers
sections.doc:
In this (technical) epilogue, we show that the "Chapter 2" natural numbers {name}`Chapter2.Nat` are
isomorphic in various senses to the standard natural numbers {lean}`ℕ`.

After this epilogue, {name}`Chapter2.Nat` will be deprecated, and we will instead use the standard
natural numbers {lean}`ℕ` throughout.  In particular, one should use the full Mathlib API for {lean}`ℕ` for
all subsequent chapters, in lieu of the {name}`Chapter2.Nat` API.

Filling the sorries here requires both the {name}`Chapter2.Nat` API and the Mathlib API for the standard
natural numbers {lean}`ℕ`.  As such, they are excellent exercises to prepare you for the aforementioned
transition.

In second half of this section we also give a fully axiomatic treatment of the natural numbers
via the Peano axioms. The treatment in the preceding three sections was only partially axiomatic,
because we used a specific construction {name}`Chapter2.Nat` of the natural numbers that was an inductive
type, and used that inductive type to construct a recursor.  Here, we give some exercises to show
how one can accomplish the same tasks directly from the Peano axioms, without knowing the specific
implementation of the natural numbers.

## Tips from past users

Users of the companion who have completed the exercises in this section are welcome to send their tips for future users in this section as PRs.

- (Add tip here)

sections.title: Section 3.1: Fundamentals (of set theory)
sections.doc:
In this section we set up a version of Zermelo-Frankel set theory (with atoms) that tries to be
as faithful as possible to the original text of Analysis I, Section 3.1. All numbering refers to
the original text.

I have attempted to make the translation as faithful a paraphrasing as possible of the original
text. When there is a choice between a more idiomatic Lean solution and a more faithful
translation, I have generally chosen the latter. In particular, there will be places where the
Lean code could be "golfed" to be more elegant and idiomatic, but I have consciously avoided
doing so.

Main constructions and results of this section:

- A type `Chapter3.SetTheory.Set` of sets
- A type `Chapter3.SetTheory.Object` of objects
- An axiom that every set is (or can be coerced into) an object
- The empty set {syntax term}`∅`, singletons {syntax term}`{y}`, and pairs {syntax term}`{y,z}` (and more general finite tuples), with
  their attendant axioms
- Pairwise union {syntax term}`X ∪ Y`, and their attendant axioms
- Coercion of a set `A` to its associated type `A.toSubtype`, which is a subtype of `Object`, and
  basic API.  (This is a technical construction needed to make the Zermelo-Frankel set theory
  compatible with the dependent type theory of Lean.)
- The specification `A.specify P` of a set `A` and a predicate `P: A.toSubtype → Prop` to the
  subset of elements of `A` obeying `P`, and the axiom of specification.
  TODO: somehow implement set builder elaboration for this.
- The replacement `A.replace hP` of a set `A` via a predicate
  `P: A.toSubtype → Object → Prop` obeying a uniqueness condition
  `∀ x y y', P x y ∧ P x y' → y = y'`, and the axiom of replacement.
- A bijective correspondence between the Mathlib natural numbers `ℕ` and a set
  `Chapter3.Nat : Chapter3.Set` (the axiom of infinity).
- Axioms of regularity, power set, and union (used in later sections of this chapter, but not
  required here)
- Connections with Mathlib's notion of a {name}`Set`

The other axioms of Zermelo-Frankel set theory are discussed in later sections.

Some technical notes:
- Mathlib of course has its own notion of a {name}`Set` (or more precisely, a type `Set X` associated to
  each type `X`), which is not compatible with the notion `Chapter3.Set` defined here,
  though we will try to make the notations match as much as possible.  This causes some notational
  conflict: for instance, one may need to explicitly specify `(∅:Chapter3.Set)` instead of just {syntax term}`∅`
  to indicate that one is using the `Chapter3.Set` version of the empty set, rather than the
  Mathlib version of the empty set, and similarly for other notation defined here.
- In Analysis I, we chose to work with an "impure" set theory, in which there could be more
  `Object`s than just `Set`s.  In the type theory of Lean, this requires treating `Chapter3.Set`
  and `Chapter3.Object` as distinct types. Occasionally this means we have to use a coercion
  `(X: Chapter3.Object)` of a `Chapter3.Set` `X` to make into a `Chapter3.Object`: this is
  mostly needed when manipulating sets of sets.
- Strictly speaking, a set `X:Set` is not a type; however, we will coerce sets to types, and
  specifically to a subtype of `Object`.  A similar coercion is in place for Mathlib's
  formalization of sets.
- After this chapter is concluded, the notion of a `Chapter3.SetTheory.Set` will be deprecated in
  favor of the standard Mathlib notion of a {name}`Set` (or more precisely of the type `Set X` of a set
  in a given type `X`).  However, due to various technical incompatibilities between set theory
  and type theory, we will not attempt to create a full equivalence between these two
  notions of sets. (As such, this makes this entire chapter optional from the point of view of
  the rest of the book, though we retain it for pedagogical purposes.)


## Tips from past users

Users of the companion who have completed the exercises in this section are welcome to send their tips for future users in this section as PRs.

- (Add tip here)

declarations.statement: theorem SetTheory.Set.ext {X Y:Set} (h: ∀ x, x ∈ X ↔ x ∈ Y) : X = Y

declarations.name: Chapter3.SetTheory.Set.not_mem_empty
declarations.doc:
Axiom 3.3 (empty set).

sections.title: Section 3.2: Russell's paradox
sections.doc:
I have attempted to make the translation as faithful a paraphrasing as possible of the original
text. When there is a choice between a more idiomatic Lean solution and a more faithful
translation, I have generally chosen the latter.  In particular, there will be places where the
Lean code could be "golfed" to be more elegant and idiomatic, but I have consciously avoided
doing so.

This section is mostly optional, though it does make explicit the axiom of foundation which is
used in a minor role in an exercise in Section 3.5.

Main constructions and results of this section:

- Russell's paradox (ruling out the axiom of universal specification).
- The axiom of regularity (foundation) - an axiom designed to avoid Russell's paradox.

## Tips from past users

Users of the companion who have completed the exercises in this section are welcome to send their tips for future users in this section as PRs.

sections.title: Section 3.3: Functions
sections.doc:
I have attempted to make the translation as faithful a paraphrasing as possible of the original
text. When there is a choice between a more idiomatic Lean solution and a more faithful
translation, I have generally chosen the latter. In particular, there will be places where the
Lean code could be "golfed" to be more elegant and idiomatic, but I have consciously avoided
doing so.

Main constructions and results of this section:

- A notion of function `Function X Y` between two sets `X`, `Y` in the set theory of Section 3.1
- Various relations with the Mathlib notion of a function `X → Y` between two types `X`, `Y`.
  (Note from Section 3.1 that every `Set` `X` can also be viewed as a subtype
  `{x : Object // x ∈ X }` of `Object`.)
- Basic function properties and operations, such as composition, one-to-one and onto functions,
  and inverses.

In the rest of the book we will deprecate the Chapter 3 version of a function, and work with the
Mathlib notion of a function instead.  Even within this section, we will switch to the Mathlib
formalism for some of the examples involving number systems such as {lean}`ℤ` or {lean}`ℝ` that have not been
implemented in the Chapter 3 framework.

We will work here with the version {name}`Nat` of the natural numbers internal to the Chapter 3 set
theory, though usually we will use coercions to then immediately translate to the Mathlib
natural numbers {lean}`ℕ`.

## Tips from past users

Users of the companion who have completed the exercises in this section are welcome to send their tips for future users in this section as PRs.

- (Add tip here)

sections.title: Section 3.4: Images and inverse images
sections.doc:
I have attempted to make the translation as faithful a paraphrasing as possible of the original
text. When there is a choice between a more idiomatic Lean solution and a more faithful
translation, I have generally chosen the latter. In particular, there will be places where the
Lean code could be "golfed" to be more elegant and idiomatic, but I have consciously avoided
doing so.

Main constructions and results of this section:

- Images and inverse images of (Mathlib) functions, within the framework of Section 3.1 set
  theory. (The Section 3.3 functions are now deprecated and will not be used further.)
- Connection with Mathlib's image {syntax term}`f '' S` and preimage {syntax term}`f ⁻¹' S` notions.

## Tips from past users

Users of the companion who have completed the exercises in this section are welcome to send their tips for future users in this section as PRs.

- (Add tip here)

declarations.name: Chapter3.SetTheory.Set.image
declarations.doc: Definition 3.4.1.  Interestingly, the definition does not require {lean}`S` to be a subset of {lean}`X`.
declarations.statement: abbrev SetTheory.Set.image {X Y:Set} (f:X → Y) (S: Set) : Set

declarations.name: Chapter3.SetTheory.Set.mem_image
declarations.statement:
theorem SetTheory.Set.mem_image {X Y:Set} (f:X → Y) (S: Set) (y:Object) :
    y ∈ image f S ↔ ∃ x:X, x.val ∈ S ∧ f x = y

declarations.name: Chapter3.f_3_4_2
declarations.statement: abbrev f_3_4_2 : nat → nat

declarations.doc: Example 3.4.3 is written using Mathlib's notion of image.

declarations.name: Chapter3.SetTheory.Set.preimage
declarations.doc:
Definition 3.4.4 (inverse images).
Again, it is not required that {lean}`U` be a subset of {lean}`Y`.
declarations.statement: abbrev SetTheory.Set.preimage {X Y:Set} (f:X → Y) (U: Set) : Set

declarations.name: Chapter3.SetTheory.Set.preimage_f_3_4_2
declarations.statement: theorem SetTheory.Set.preimage_f_3_4_2 : preimage f_3_4_2 {2,4,6} = {1,2,3}

declarations.doc: Example 3.4.7 (using the Mathlib notion of preimage)

declarations.name: Chapter3.SetTheory.Set.powerset_axiom
declarations.statement:
theorem SetTheory.Set.powerset_axiom {X Y:Set} (F:Object) :
    F ∈ (X ^ Y) ↔ ∃ f: Y → X, f = F

declarations.name: Chapter3.SetTheory.Set.powerset
declarations.doc: Exercise 3.4.6 (i). One needs to provide a suitable definition of the power set here.
declarations.statement: def SetTheory.Set.powerset (X:Set) : Set

declarations.name: Chapter3.SetTheory.Set.mem_powerset
declarations.statement:
theorem SetTheory.Set.mem_powerset {X:Set} (x:Object) :
    x ∈ powerset X ↔ ∃ Y:Set, x = Y ∧ Y ⊆ X

declarations.name: Chapter3.SetTheory.Set.exists_powerset
declarations.statement:
theorem SetTheory.Set.exists_powerset (X:Set) :
   ∃ (Z: Set), ∀ x, x ∈ Z ↔ ∃ Y:Set, x = Y ∧ Y ⊆ X

declarations.name: Chapter3.SetTheory.Set.powerset_of_triple
declarations.statement:
theorem SetTheory.Set.powerset_of_triple (a b c x:Object) :
    x ∈ powerset {a,b,c}
    ↔ x = (∅:Set)
    ∨ x = ({a}:Set)
    ∨ x = ({b}:Set)
    ∨ x = ({c}:Set)
    ∨ x = ({a,b}:Set)
    ∨ x = ({a,c}:Set)
    ∨ x = ({b,c}:Set)
    ∨ x = ({a,b,c}:Set)

declarations.name: Chapter3.SetTheory.Set.union_axiom
declarations.statement:
theorem SetTheory.Set.union_axiom (A: Set) (x:Object) :
    x ∈ union A ↔ ∃ (S:Set), x ∈ S ∧ (S:Object) ∈ A

declarations.name: Chapter3.SetTheory.Set.example_3_4_12
declarations.statement:
theorem SetTheory.Set.example_3_4_12 :
    union { (({2,3}:Set):Object), (({3,4}:Set):Object), (({4,5}:Set):Object) } = {2,3,4,5}

declarations.name: Chapter3.SetTheory.Set.preimage_eq_image_of_inv
declarations.statement:
theorem SetTheory.Set.preimage_eq_image_of_inv {X Y V:Set} (f:X → Y) (f_inv: Y → X)
  (hf: Function.LeftInverse f_inv f ∧ Function.RightInverse f_inv f) (hV: V ⊆ Y) :
    image f_inv V = preimage f V

declarations.name: Chapter3.SetTheory.Set.image_of_inter
declarations.statement:
theorem SetTheory.Set.image_of_inter {X Y:Set} (f:X → Y) (A B: Set) :
    image f (A ∩ B) ⊆ (image f A) ∩ (image f B)

declarations.name: Chapter3.SetTheory.Set.preimage_of_inter
declarations.statement:
theorem SetTheory.Set.preimage_of_inter {X Y:Set} (f:X → Y) (A B: Set) :
    preimage f (A ∩ B) = (preimage f A) ∩ (preimage f B)

declarations.name: Chapter3.SetTheory.Set.image_preimage_of_surj
declarations.statement:
theorem SetTheory.Set.image_preimage_of_surj {X Y:Set} (f:X → Y) :
    (∀ S, S ⊆ Y → image f (preimage f S) = S) ↔ Function.Surjective f

declarations.name: Chapter3.SetTheory.Set.preimage_image_of_inj
declarations.statement:
theorem SetTheory.Set.preimage_image_of_inj {X Y:Set} (f:X → Y) :
    (∀ S, S ⊆ X → preimage f (image f S) = S) ↔ Function.Injective f

declarations.name: Chapter3.SetTheory.Set.partial_functions
declarations.statement:
theorem SetTheory.Set.partial_functions {X Y:Set} :
    ∃ Z:Set, ∀ F:Object, F ∈ Z ↔ ∃ X' Y':Set, X' ⊆ X ∧ Y' ⊆ Y ∧ ∃ f: X' → Y', F = f

declarations.name: Chapter3.SetTheory.Set.union_pair_exists
declarations.doc:
Exercise 3.4.8.  The point of this exercise is to prove it without using the
pairwise union operation {kw (of := «term_∪_»)}`∪`.
declarations.statement: theorem SetTheory.Set.union_pair_exists (X Y:Set) : ∃ Z:Set, ∀ x, x ∈ Z ↔ (x ∈ X ∨ x ∈ Y)

declarations.name: Chapter3.SetTheory.Set.iInter'_insensitive
declarations.statement:
theorem SetTheory.Set.iInter'_insensitive {I:Set} (β β':I) (A: I → Set) :
    iInter' I β A = iInter' I β' A

declarations.name: Chapter3.SetTheory.Set.union_iUnion
declarations.doc: Exercise 3.4.10 (union over a union of index sets)
declarations.statement:
theorem SetTheory.Set.union_iUnion {I J:Set} (A: (I ∪ J:Set) → Set) :
    iUnion I (fun α ↦ A ⟨ α.val, by simp [α.property]⟩)
    ∪ iUnion J (fun α ↦ A ⟨ α.val, by simp [α.property]⟩)
    = iUnion (I ∪ J) A

declarations.name: Chapter3.SetTheory.Set.union_of_nonempty
declarations.doc: Exercise 3.4.10 (a union of nonempty index sets is nonempty)
declarations.statement: theorem SetTheory.Set.union_of_nonempty {I J:Set} (hI: I ≠ ∅) (hJ: J ≠ ∅) : I ∪ J ≠ ∅

declarations.name: Chapter3.SetTheory.Set.inter_iInter
declarations.doc: Exercise 3.4.10 (intersection over a union of index sets)
declarations.statement:
theorem SetTheory.Set.inter_iInter {I J:Set} (hI: I ≠ ∅) (hJ: J ≠ ∅) (A: (I ∪ J:Set) → Set) :
    iInter I hI (fun α ↦ A ⟨ α.val, by simp [α.property]⟩)
    ∩ iInter J hJ (fun α ↦ A ⟨ α.val, by simp [α.property]⟩)
    = iInter (I ∪ J) (union_of_nonempty hI hJ) A

declarations.name: Chapter3.SetTheory.Set.compl_iUnion
declarations.statement:
theorem SetTheory.Set.compl_iUnion {X I: Set} (hI: I ≠ ∅) (A: I → Set) :
    X \ iUnion I A = iInter I hI (fun α ↦ X \ A α)

declarations.name: Chapter3.SetTheory.Set.compl_iInter
declarations.statement:
theorem SetTheory.Set.compl_iInter {X I: Set} (hI: I ≠ ∅) (A: I → Set) :
    X \ iInter I hI A = iUnion I (fun α ↦ X \ A α)

sections.title: Section 3.5: Cartesian products
sections.doc:
I have attempted to make the translation as faithful a paraphrasing as possible of the original
text. When there is a choice between a more idiomatic Lean solution and a more faithful
translation, I have generally chosen the latter. In particular, there will be places where the
Lean code could be "golfed" to be more elegant and idiomatic, but I have consciously avoided
doing so.

Main constructions and results of this section:

- Ordered pairs and n-tuples.
- Cartesian products and n-fold products.
- Finite choice.
- Connections with Mathlib counterparts such as {name}`Set.pi` and {name}`Set.prod`.

## Tips from past users

See Exercise 3.5.10 below for some connections between this concept and the preceding notion

declarations.name: Chapter3.SetTheory.Set.iProd

declarations.name: Chapter3.SetTheory.Set.prod_union
declarations.statement: theorem SetTheory.Set.prod_union (A B C:Set) : A ×ˢ (B ∪ C) = (A ×ˢ B) ∪ (A ×ˢ C)

declarations.name: Chapter3.SetTheory.Set.iProd_empty_iff
declarations.statement:
theorem SetTheory.Set.iProd_empty_iff {n:ℕ} {X: Fin n → Set} :

declarations.name: Chapter3.SetTheory.Set.iUnion_inter_iUnion
declarations.statement:
theorem SetTheory.Set.iUnion_inter_iUnion {I J: Set} (A: I → Set) (B: J → Set) :

theorem SetTheory.Set.graph_inj {X Y:Set} (f f': X → Y) :

declarations.name: Chapter3.SetTheory.Set.powerset_axiom'
declarations.doc:
Exercise 3.5.11. This trivially follows from {name}`SetTheory.Set.powerset_axiom`, but the
exercise is to derive it from {name}`SetTheory.Set.exists_powerset` instead.
declarations.statement:
theorem SetTheory.Set.powerset_axiom' (X Y:Set) :
    ∃! S:Set, ∀(F:Object), F ∈ S ↔ ∃ f: Y → X, f = F

declarations.name: Chapter3.SetTheory.Set.recursion
declarations.doc: Exercise 3.5.12, with errata from web site incorporated
declarations.statement:
theorem SetTheory.Set.recursion (X: Set) (f: nat → X → X) (c:X) :
    ∃! a: nat → X, a 0 = c ∧ ∀ n, a (n + 1:ℕ) = f n (a n)

declarations.name: Chapter3.SetTheory.Set.nat_unique
declarations.statement:
theorem SetTheory.Set.nat_unique (nat':Set) (zero:nat') (succ:nat' → nat')
  (succ_ne: ∀ n:nat', succ n ≠ zero) (succ_of_ne: ∀ n m:nat', n ≠ m → succ n ≠ succ m)
  (ind: ∀ P: nat' → Prop, P zero → (∀ n, P n → P (succ n)) → ∀ n, P n) :
    ∃! f : nat → nat', Function.Bijective f ∧ f 0 = zero
    ∧ ∀ (n:nat) (n':nat'), f n = n' ↔ f (n+1:ℕ) = succ n'

sections.title: Section 3.6: Cardinality of sets

I have attempted to make the translation as faithful a paraphrasing as possible of the original

Lean code could be "golfed" to be more elegant and idiomatic, but I have consciously avoided

Main constructions and results of this section:

- Cardinality of a set
- Finite and infinite sets
- Connections with Mathlib equivalents

After this section, these notions will be deprecated in favor of their Mathlib equivalents.

sections.title: Chapter 3 epilogue: Connections with ZFSet
sections.doc:
In this epilogue we show that the {name}`ZFSet` type in Mathlib (derived as a quotient from the
{name}`PSet` type) can be used to create models of the `SetTheory` class studied in this chapter, so long as we work in a universe of level at
least 1.  The constructions here are due to Edward van de Meent; see
https://leanprover.zulipchat.com/#narrow/channel/113489-new-members/topic/Can.20this.20proof.20related.20to.20Set.20replacement.20be.20shorter.3F/near/527305173

sections.title: Section 4.1: The integers
sections.doc:
I have attempted to make the translation as faithful a paraphrasing as possible of the original
text. When there is a choice between a more idiomatic Lean solution and a more faithful
translation, I have generally chosen the latter. In particular, there will be places where the
Lean code could be "golfed" to be more elegant and idiomatic, but I have consciously avoided
doing so.

Main constructions and results of this section:

- Definition of the "Section 4.1" integers, `Section_4_1.Int`, as formal differences `a —— b` of
  natural numbers `a b:ℕ`, up to equivalence.  (This is a quotient of a scaffolding type
  `Section_4_1.PreInt`, which consists of formal differences without any equivalence imposed.)

- ring operations and order these integers, as well as an embedding of {lean}`ℕ`.

- Equivalence with the Mathlib integers {name}`_root_.Int` (or {lean}`ℤ`), which we will use going forward.

sections.title: Section 4.2

This file is a translation of Section 4.2 of Analysis I to Lean 4.
All numbering refers to the original text.

I have attempted to make the translation as faithful a paraphrasing as possible of the original
text. When there is a choice between a more idiomatic Lean solution and a more faithful
translation, I have generally chosen the latter. In particular, there will be places where the
Lean code could be "golfed" to be more elegant and idiomatic, but I have consciously avoided
doing so.

Main constructions and results of this section:

- Definition of the "Section 4.2" rationals, `Section_4_2.Rat`, as formal quotients `a // b` of
  integers `a b:ℤ`, up to equivalence.  (This is a quotient of a scaffolding type
  `Section_4_2.PreRat`, which consists of formal quotients without any equivalence imposed.)

- Field operations and order on these rationals, as well as an embedding of {lean}`ℕ` and {lean}`ℤ`.

- Equivalence with the Mathlib rationals {name}`_root_.Rat` (or {lean}`ℚ`), which we will use going forward.

Note: here (and in the sequel) we use Mathlib's natural numbers {lean}`ℕ` and integers {lean}`ℤ` rather than
the Chapter 2 natural numbers and Section 4.1 integers.

## Tips from past users

sections.title: Section 4.3: Absolute value and exponentiation
sections.doc:
I have attempted to make the translation as faithful a paraphrasing as possible of the original
text. When there is a choice between a more idiomatic Lean solution and a more faithful
translation, I have generally chosen the latter.  In particular, there will be places where the
Lean code could be "golfed" to be more elegant and idiomatic, but I have consciously avoided
doing so.

Main constructions and results of this section:

- Basic properties of absolute value and exponentiation on the rational numbers (here we use the
  Mathlib rational numbers {lean}`ℚ` rather than the Section 4.2 rational numbers).

Note: to avoid notational conflict, we are using the standard Mathlib definitions of absolute
value and exponentiation.  As such, it is possible to solve several of the exercises here rather
easily using the Mathlib API for these operations.  However, the spirit of the exercises is to
solve these instead using the API provided in this section, as well as more basic Mathlib API for
the rational numbers that does not reference either absolute value or exponentiation.

## Tips from past users

Users of the companion who have completed the exercises in this section are welcome to send their tips for future users in this section as PRs.

- (Add tip here)

declarations.name: Section_4_3.abs_of_zero
declarations.statement: theorem abs_of_zero : abs 0 = 0

declarations.name: Section_4_3.dist_eq
declarations.doc:
Definition 4.3.2 (Distance).
We avoid the Mathlib notion of distance here because it is real-valued.
declarations.statement: theorem dist_eq (x y: ℚ) : dist x y = |x-y|

declarations.name: Section_4_3.abs_nonneg
declarations.statement: theorem abs_nonneg (x: ℚ) : |x| ≥ 0

declarations.name: Section_4_3.abs_eq_zero_iff
declarations.statement: theorem abs_eq_zero_iff (x: ℚ) : |x| = 0 ↔ x = 0

declarations.name: Section_4_3.abs_add
declarations.statement: theorem abs_add (x y:ℚ) : |x + y| ≤ |x| + |y|

declarations.name: Section_4_3.abs_le_iff
declarations.statement: theorem abs_le_iff (x y:ℚ) : -y ≤ x ∧ x ≤ y ↔ |x| ≤ y

declarations.name: Section_4_3.le_abs
declarations.doc: Proposition 4.3.3(c) (bounded by own absolute value) / Exercise 4.3.1
declarations.statement: theorem le_abs (x:ℚ) : -|x| ≤ x ∧ x ≤ |x|

declarations.name: Section_4_3.abs_mul
declarations.statement: theorem abs_mul (x y:ℚ) : |x * y| = |x| * |y|

declarations.name: Section_4_3.abs_neg
declarations.statement: theorem abs_neg (x:ℚ) : |-x| = |x|

declarations.name: Section_4_3.dist_nonneg
declarations.statement: theorem dist_nonneg (x y:ℚ) : dist x y ≥ 0

declarations.name: Section_4_3.dist_eq_zero_iff
declarations.statement: theorem dist_eq_zero_iff (x y:ℚ) : dist x y = 0 ↔ x = y

declarations.name: Section_4_3.dist_symm
declarations.statement: theorem dist_symm (x y:ℚ) : dist x y = dist y x

declarations.name: Section_4_3.dist_le
declarations.statement: theorem dist_le (x y z:ℚ) : dist x z ≤ dist x y + dist y z

declarations.name: Section_4_3.close_iff
declarations.doc:
Definition 4.3.4 (eps-closeness).  In the text the notion is undefined for ε zero or negative,
but it is more convenient in Lean to assign a "junk" definition in this case.  But this also
allows some relaxations of hypotheses in the lemmas that follow.
declarations.statement: theorem close_iff (ε x y:ℚ): ε.Close x y ↔ |x - y| ≤ ε
example : (0.1:ℚ).Close (0.99:ℚ) (1.01:ℚ)
example (ε : ℚ) (hε : ε > 0) : ε.Close 2 2

declarations.name: Section_4_3.eq_if_close
declarations.statement: theorem eq_if_close (x y:ℚ) : x = y ↔ ∀ ε:ℚ, ε > 0 → ε.Close x y

declarations.name: Section_4_3.close_symm
declarations.statement: theorem close_symm (ε x y:ℚ) : ε.Close x y ↔ ε.Close y x

declarations.name: Section_4_3.close_trans
declarations.statement:
theorem close_trans {ε δ x y z:ℚ} (hxy: ε.Close x y) (hyz: δ.Close y z) :
    (ε + δ).Close x z

declarations.name: Section_4_3.add_close
declarations.statement:
theorem add_close {ε δ x y z w:ℚ} (hxy: ε.Close x y) (hzw: δ.Close z w) :
    (ε + δ).Close (x+z) (y+w)

declarations.name: Section_4_3.sub_close
declarations.statement:
theorem sub_close {ε δ x y z w:ℚ} (hxy: ε.Close x y) (hzw: δ.Close z w) :
    (ε + δ).Close (x-z) (y-w)

declarations.name: Section_4_3.close_mono
declarations.statement:
theorem close_mono {ε ε' x y:ℚ} (hxy: ε.Close x y) (hε: ε' ≥  ε) :
    ε'.Close x y

declarations.name: Section_4_3.close_between
declarations.statement:
theorem close_between {ε x y z w:ℚ} (hxy: ε.Close x y) (hxz: ε.Close x z)
  (hbetween: (y ≤ w ∧ w ≤ z) ∨ (z ≤ w ∧ w ≤ y)) : ε.Close x w

declarations.name: Section_4_3.close_mul_right
declarations.statement:
theorem close_mul_right {ε x y z:ℚ} (hxy: ε.Close x y) :
    (ε*|z|).Close (x * z) (y * z)

declarations.name: Section_4_3.close_mul_mul
declarations.statement:
theorem close_mul_mul {ε δ x y z w:ℚ} (hxy: ε.Close x y) (hzw: δ.Close z w) :
    (ε*|z|+δ*|x|+ε*δ).Close (x * z) (y * w)

declarations.name: Section_4_3.pow_zero
declarations.doc: Definition 4.3.9 (exponentiation) (base case).  Here we use the Mathlib definition.
declarations.statement: lemma pow_zero (x:ℚ) : x^0 = 1

declarations.name: Section_4_3.pow_succ
declarations.doc: Definition 4.3.9 (exponentiation) (inductive step).  Here we use the Mathlib definition.
declarations.statement: lemma pow_succ (x:ℚ) (n:ℕ) : x^(n+1) = x^n * x

declarations.name: Section_4_3.pow_add
declarations.doc: Proposition 4.3.10(a) (Properties of exponentiation, I) (exponent sum) / Exercise 4.3.3
declarations.statement: theorem pow_add (x:ℚ) (m n:ℕ) : x^n * x^m = x^(n+m)

declarations.name: Section_4_3.pow_mul
declarations.doc: Proposition 4.3.10(a) (Properties of exponentiation, I) (exponent product) / Exercise 4.3.3
declarations.statement: theorem pow_mul (x:ℚ) (m n:ℕ) : (x^n)^m = x^(n*m)

declarations.name: Section_4_3.mul_pow
declarations.doc: Proposition 4.3.10(a) (Properties of exponentiation, I) (product base) / Exercise 4.3.3
declarations.statement: theorem mul_pow (x y:ℚ) (n:ℕ) : (x*y)^n = x^n * y^n

declarations.name: Section_4_3.pow_eq_zero
declarations.statement: theorem pow_eq_zero (x:ℚ) (n:ℕ) (hn : 0 < n) : x^n = 0 ↔ x = 0

declarations.name: Section_4_3.pow_nonneg
declarations.statement: theorem pow_nonneg {x:ℚ} (n:ℕ) (hx: x ≥ 0) : x^n ≥ 0

declarations.name: Section_4_3.pow_pos
declarations.statement: theorem pow_pos {x:ℚ} (n:ℕ) (hx: x > 0) : x^n > 0

declarations.name: Section_4_3.pow_ge_pow
declarations.statement: theorem pow_ge_pow (x y:ℚ) (n:ℕ) (hxy: x ≥ y) (hy: y ≥ 0) : x^n ≥ y^n

declarations.name: Section_4_3.pow_gt_pow
declarations.doc: Proposition 4.3.10(c) (Properties of exponentiation, I) (strict inequality) / Exercise 4.3.3
declarations.statement: theorem pow_gt_pow (x y:ℚ) (n:ℕ) (hxy: x > y) (hy: y ≥ 0) (hn: n > 0) : x^n > y^n

declarations.name: Section_4_3.pow_abs
declarations.statement: theorem pow_abs (x:ℚ) (n:ℕ) : |x|^n = |x^n|

declarations.name: Section_4_3.zpow_neg
declarations.doc:
Definition 4.3.11 (Exponentiation to a negative number).
Here we use the Mathlib notion of integer exponentiation
declarations.statement: theorem zpow_neg (x:ℚ) (n:ℕ) : x^(-(n:ℤ)) = 1/(x^n)

declarations.name: Section_4_3.zpow_add
declarations.doc: Proposition 4.3.12(a) (Properties of exponentiation, II) (exponent sum) / Exercise 4.3.4
declarations.statement: theorem zpow_add (x:ℚ) (n m:ℤ) (hx: x ≠ 0): x^n * x^m = x^(n+m)

declarations.name: Section_4_3.zpow_mul
declarations.doc: Proposition 4.3.12(a) (Properties of exponentiation, II) (exponent product) / Exercise 4.3.4
declarations.statement: theorem zpow_mul (x:ℚ) (n m:ℤ) : (x^n)^m = x^(n*m)

declarations.name: Section_4_3.mul_zpow
declarations.doc: Proposition 4.3.12(a) (Properties of exponentiation, II) (product base) / Exercise 4.3.4
declarations.statement: theorem mul_zpow (x y:ℚ) (n:ℤ) : (x*y)^n = x^n * y^n

declarations.name: Section_4_3.zpow_pos
declarations.statement: theorem zpow_pos {x:ℚ} (n:ℤ) (hx: x > 0) : x^n > 0

declarations.name: Section_4_3.zpow_ge_zpow
declarations.statement: theorem zpow_ge_zpow {x y:ℚ} {n:ℤ} (hxy: x ≥ y) (hy: y > 0) (hn: n > 0): x^n ≥ y^n

declarations.name: Section_4_3.zpow_inj
declarations.statement: theorem zpow_inj {x y:ℚ} {n:ℤ} (hx: x > 0) (hy : y > 0) (hn: n ≠ 0) (hxy: x^n = y^n) : x = y

declarations.name: Section_4_3.zpow_abs
declarations.statement: theorem zpow_abs (x:ℚ) (n:ℤ) : |x|^n = |x^n|

declarations.name: Section_4_3.two_pow_geq
declarations.statement: theorem two_pow_geq (N:ℕ) : 2^N ≥ N

sections.title: Section 4.4: gaps in the rational numbers
sections.doc:
I have attempted to make the translation as faithful a paraphrasing as possible of the original
text. When there is a choice between a more idiomatic Lean solution and a more faithful
translation, I have generally chosen the latter.  In particular, there will be places where the
Lean code could be "golfed" to be more elegant and idiomatic, but I have consciously avoided
doing so.

Main constructions and results of this section:

- Irrationality of √2, and related facts about the rational numbers

Many of the results here can be established more quickly by relying more heavily on the Mathlib
API; one can set oneself the exercise of doing so.

## Tips from past users

Users of the companion who have completed the exercises in this section are welcome to send their tips for future users in this section as PRs.

declarations.name: Rat.between_int
declarations.doc: Proposition 4.4.1 (Interspersing of integers by rationals) / Exercise 4.4.1
declarations.statement: theorem Rat.between_int (x:ℚ) : ∃! n:ℤ, n ≤ x ∧ x < n+1

declarations.name: Rat.exists_between_rat
declarations.statement: theorem Rat.exists_between_rat {x y:ℚ} (h: x < y) : ∃ z:ℚ, x < z ∧ z < y

declarations.name: Nat.no_infinite_descent
declarations.statement: theorem Nat.no_infinite_descent : ¬ ∃ a:ℕ → ℕ, ∀ n, a (n+1) < a n

declarations.name: Int.infinite_descent
declarations.statement: def Int.infinite_descent : Decidable (∃ a:ℕ → ℤ, ∀ n, a (n+1) < a n)

declarations.name: Rat.pos_infinite_descent
declarations.statement: def Rat.pos_infinite_descent : Decidable (∃ a:ℕ → {x: ℚ // 0 < x}, ∀ n, a (n+1) < a n)

declarations.name: Rat.not_exist_sqrt_two
declarations.statement: theorem Rat.not_exist_sqrt_two : ¬ ∃ x:ℚ, x^2 = 2

declarations.name: Rat.exist_approx_sqrt_two
declarations.statement: theorem Rat.exist_approx_sqrt_two {ε:ℚ} (hε:ε>0) : ∃ x ≥ (0:ℚ), x^2 < 2 ∧ 2 < (x+ε)^2

sections.title: Section 5.1: Cauchy sequences
sections.doc:
I have attempted to make the translation as faithful a paraphrasing as possible of the original

Lean code could be "golfed" to be more elegant and idiomatic, but I have consciously avoided

Main constructions and results of this section:

- Notion of a sequence of rationals
- Notions of `ε`-steadiness, eventual `ε`-steadiness, and Cauchy sequences

## Tips from past users

Users of the companion who have completed the exercises in this section are welcome to send their tips for future users in this section as PRs.

- (Add tip here)

declarations.name: Chapter5.Sequence
declarations.doc:
Definition 5.1.1 (Sequence). To avoid some technicalities involving dependent types, we extend
sequences by zero to the left of the starting point {name (full := Sequence.n₀)}`n₀`.
declarations.statement: structure Sequence

declarations.name: Chapter5.Sequence.squares
declarations.statement: abbrev Sequence.squares : Sequence
example (n:ℕ) : Sequence.squares n = n^2

declarations.name: Chapter5.Sequence.three
declarations.statement: abbrev Sequence.three : Sequence
example (n:ℕ) : Sequence.three n = 3

declarations.name: Chapter5.Sequence.squares_from_three
declarations.statement: abbrev Sequence.squares_from_three : Sequence
example (n:ℤ) (hn: n ≥ 3) : Sequence.squares_from_three n = n^2

declarations.name: Chapter5.Rat.Steady.coe
declarations.doc: Definition 5.1.3 - definition of {name}`ε`-steadiness for a sequence starting at 0
declarations.statement:
lemma Rat.Steady.coe (ε : ℚ) (a:ℕ → ℚ) :
    ε.Steady a ↔ ∀ n m : ℕ, ε.Close (a n) (a m)
example : (1:ℚ).Steady ((fun n:ℕ ↦ if Even n then (1:ℚ) else (0:ℚ)):Sequence)

declarations.doc: Example 5.1.5: The sequence `1, 0, 1, 0, ...` is not ½-steady.
declarations.statement: example : ¬ (0.5:ℚ).Steady ((fun n:ℕ ↦ if Even n then (1:ℚ) else (0:ℚ)):Sequence)
example : (0.1:ℚ).Steady ((fun n:ℕ ↦ (10:ℚ) ^ (-(n:ℤ)-1) ):Sequence)

declarations.doc: Example 5.1.5: The sequence 0.1, 0.01, 0.001, ... is not 0.01-steady. Left as an exercise.
declarations.statement: example : ¬(0.01:ℚ).Steady ((fun n:ℕ ↦ (10:ℚ) ^ (-(n:ℤ)-1) ):Sequence)

declarations.doc: Example 5.1.5: The sequence 1, 2, 4, 8, ... is not ε-steady for any ε. Left as an exercise.
declarations.statement: example (ε:ℚ) : ¬ ε.Steady ((fun n:ℕ ↦ (2 ^ (n+1):ℚ) ):Sequence)

declarations.doc: Example 5.1.5:The sequence 2, 2, 2, ... is ε-steady for any ε > 0.
declarations.statement: example (ε:ℚ) (hε: ε>0) : ε.Steady ((fun _:ℕ ↦ (2:ℚ) ):Sequence)

declarations.name: Rat.EventuallySteady
declarations.statement: abbrev Rat.EventuallySteady (ε: ℚ) (a: Chapter5.Sequence) : Prop

declarations.name: Chapter5.Sequence.ex_5_1_7_a
declarations.statement: lemma Sequence.ex_5_1_7_a : ¬ (0.1:ℚ).Steady ((fun n:ℕ ↦ (n+1:ℚ)⁻¹ ):Sequence)

declarations.name: Chapter5.Sequence.ex_5_1_7_b
declarations.doc: Example 5.1.7: The sequence `a_10, a_11, a_12, ...` is 0.1-steady
declarations.statement: lemma Sequence.ex_5_1_7_b : (0.1:ℚ).Steady (((fun n:ℕ ↦ (n+1:ℚ)⁻¹ ):Sequence).from 10)

declarations.name: Chapter5.Sequence.ex_5_1_7_c
declarations.statement: lemma Sequence.ex_5_1_7_c : (0.1:ℚ).EventuallySteady ((fun n:ℕ ↦ (n+1:ℚ)⁻¹ ):Sequence)

declarations.name: Chapter5.Sequence.ex_5_1_7_d
declarations.doc:
Example 5.1.7

The sequence 10, 0, 0, ... is eventually ε-steady for every ε > 0. Left as an exercise.
declarations.statement:
lemma Sequence.ex_5_1_7_d {ε:ℚ} (hε:ε>0) :
    ε.EventuallySteady ((fun n:ℕ ↦ if n=0 then (10:ℚ) else (0:ℚ) ):Sequence)

declarations.name: Chapter5.Sequence.ex_5_1_10_a
declarations.doc: Example 5.1.10. (This requires extensive familiarity with Mathlib's API for the real numbers.)
declarations.statement: theorem Sequence.ex_5_1_10_a : (1:ℚ).Steady sqrt_two

declarations.name: Chapter5.Sequence.ex_5_1_10_b
declarations.doc: Example 5.1.10. (This requires extensive familiarity with Mathlib's API for the real numbers.)
declarations.statement: theorem Sequence.ex_5_1_10_b : (0.1:ℚ).Steady (sqrt_two.from 1)

declarations.name: Chapter5.Sequence.IsCauchy.harmonic
declarations.doc: Proposition 5.1.11. The harmonic sequence, defined as a₁ = 1, a₂ = 1/2, ... is a Cauchy sequence.
declarations.statement: theorem Sequence.IsCauchy.harmonic : (mk' 1 (fun n ↦ (1:ℚ)/n)).IsCauchy

declarations.name: Chapter5.boundedBy_def
declarations.doc:
Definition 5.1.12 (bounded sequences). Here we start sequences from {lean}`0` rather than {lean}`1` to align
better with Mathlib conventions.
declarations.statement: lemma boundedBy_def {n:ℕ} (a: Fin n → ℚ) (M:ℚ) : BoundedBy a M ↔ ∀ i, |a i| ≤ M

declarations.name: Chapter5.Sequence.boundedBy_def
declarations.statement: lemma Sequence.boundedBy_def (a:Sequence) (M:ℚ) : a.BoundedBy M ↔ ∀ n, |a n| ≤ M

declarations.name: Chapter5.Sequence.isBounded_def
declarations.statement: lemma Sequence.isBounded_def (a:Sequence) : a.IsBounded ↔ ∃ M ≥ 0, a.BoundedBy M
example : BoundedBy ![1,-2,3,-4] 4
example : ¬((fun n:ℕ ↦ (-1)^n * (n+1:ℚ)):Sequence).IsBounded
example : ((fun n:ℕ ↦ (-1:ℚ)^n):Sequence).IsBounded
example : ¬((fun n:ℕ ↦ (-1:ℚ)^n):Sequence).IsCauchy

declarations.name: Chapter5.IsBounded.finite
declarations.statement: lemma IsBounded.finite {n:ℕ} (a: Fin n → ℚ) : ∃ M ≥ 0,  BoundedBy a M

declarations.name: Chapter5.Sequence.isBounded_of_isCauchy
declarations.statement: lemma Sequence.isBounded_of_isCauchy {a:Sequence} (h: a.IsCauchy) : a.IsBounded

declarations.name: Chapter5.Sequence.isBounded_add
declarations.statement:
theorem Sequence.isBounded_add {a b:ℕ → ℚ} (ha: (a:Sequence).IsBounded) (hb: (b:Sequence).IsBounded):
    (a + b:Sequence).IsBounded

sections.title: Section 5.2: Equivalent Cauchy sequences
sections.doc:

Main constructions and results of this section:

declarations.name: Chapter5.Rat.closeSeq_def
declarations.statement:
lemma Rat.closeSeq_def (ε: ℚ) (a b: Sequence) :
    ε.CloseSeq a b ↔ ∀ n, n ≥ a.n₀ → n ≥ b.n₀ → ε.Close (a n) (b n)

example : (0.1:ℚ).CloseSeq ((fun n:ℕ ↦ ((-1)^n:ℚ)):Sequence)
((fun n:ℕ ↦ ((1.1:ℚ) * (-1)^n)):Sequence)
example : ¬ (0.1:ℚ).Steady ((fun n:ℕ ↦ ((-1)^n:ℚ)):Sequence)
example : ¬ (0.1:ℚ).Steady ((fun n:ℕ ↦ ((1.1:ℚ) * (-1)^n)):Sequence)

declarations.name: Chapter5.Rat.eventuallyClose_def
declarations.statement:
lemma Rat.eventuallyClose_def (ε: ℚ) (a b: Sequence) :
    ε.EventuallyClose a b ↔ ∃ N, ε.CloseSeq (a.from N) (b.from N)

declarations.name: Chapter5.Rat.eventuallyClose_iff
declarations.statement:
lemma Rat.eventuallyClose_iff (ε: ℚ) (a b: ℕ → ℚ) :
    ε.EventuallyClose (a:Sequence) (b:Sequence) ↔ ∃ N, ∀ n ≥ N, |a n - b n| ≤ ε

example : ¬ (0.1:ℚ).CloseSeq ((fun n:ℕ ↦ (1:ℚ)+10^(-(n:ℤ)-1)):Sequence)
  ((fun n:ℕ ↦ (1:ℚ)-10^(-(n:ℤ)-1)):Sequence)

declarations.name: Chapter5.Sequence.Equiv
declarations.statement: abbrev Sequence.Equiv (a b: ℕ → ℚ) : Prop

declarations.name: Chapter5.Sequence.equiv_def
declarations.statement:
lemma Sequence.equiv_def (a b: ℕ → ℚ) :
    Equiv a b ↔ ∀ (ε:ℚ), ε > 0 → ε.EventuallyClose (a:Sequence) (b:Sequence)

declarations.name: Chapter5.Sequence.equiv_iff
declarations.statement: lemma Sequence.equiv_iff (a b: ℕ → ℚ) : Equiv a b ↔ ∀ ε > 0, ∃ N, ∀ n ≥ N, |a n - b n| ≤ ε

declarations.name: Chapter5.Sequence.equiv_example
declarations.statement:
lemma Sequence.equiv_example :
  -- This proof is perhaps more complicated than it needs to be; a shorter version may be
  -- possible that is still faithful to the original text.
  Equiv (fun n:ℕ ↦ (1:ℚ)+10^(-(n:ℤ)-1)) (fun n:ℕ ↦ (1:ℚ)-10^(-(n:ℤ)-1))

declarations.name: Chapter5.Sequence.isCauchy_of_equiv
declarations.statement:
theorem Sequence.isCauchy_of_equiv {a b: ℕ → ℚ} (hab: Equiv a b) :
    (a:Sequence).IsCauchy ↔ (b:Sequence).IsCauchy

declarations.name: Chapter5.Sequence.isBounded_of_eventuallyClose
declarations.statement:
theorem Sequence.isBounded_of_eventuallyClose {ε:ℚ} {a b: ℕ → ℚ} (hab: ε.EventuallyClose a b) :
    (a:Sequence).IsBounded ↔ (b:Sequence).IsBounded

declarations.name: Chapter5.Sequence.equiv_trans
declarations.statement:
theorem Sequence.equiv_trans {a b c:ℕ → ℚ} (hab: Equiv a b) (hbc: Equiv b c) :
  Equiv a c

declarations.name: Chapter5.CauchySequence.instSetoid
declarations.statement: instance CauchySequence.instSetoid : Setoid CauchySequence

declarations.name: Chapter5.Real.eq_lim
declarations.statement: theorem Real.eq_lim (x:Real) : ∃ (a:ℕ → ℚ), (a:Sequence).IsCauchy ∧ x = LIM a

declarations.name: Chapter5.Real.LIM_eq_LIM
declarations.statement:
theorem Real.LIM_eq_LIM {a b:ℕ → ℚ} (ha: (a:Sequence).IsCauchy) (hb: (b:Sequence).IsCauchy) :
  LIM a = LIM b ↔ Sequence.Equiv a b

declarations.name: Chapter5.Sequence.IsCauchy.add
declarations.doc: Lemma 5.3.6 (Sum of Cauchy sequences is Cauchy).
declarations.statement:
theorem Sequence.IsCauchy.add {a b:ℕ → ℚ}  (ha: (a:Sequence).IsCauchy) (hb: (b:Sequence).IsCauchy) :
    (a + b:Sequence).IsCauchy

declarations.name: Chapter5.Sequence.add_equiv_left
declarations.doc: Lemma 5.3.7 (Sum of equivalent sequences is equivalent, left).
declarations.statement:
theorem Sequence.add_equiv_left {a a':ℕ → ℚ} (b:ℕ → ℚ) (haa': Equiv a a') :
    Equiv (a + b) (a' + b)

declarations.name: Chapter5.Sequence.add_equiv_right
declarations.doc: Lemma 5.3.7 (Sum of equivalent sequences is equivalent, right).
declarations.statement:
theorem Sequence.add_equiv_right {b b':ℕ → ℚ} (a:ℕ → ℚ) (hbb': Equiv b b') :
    Equiv (a + b) (a + b')

declarations.name: Chapter5.Sequence.add_equiv
declarations.doc: Lemma 5.3.7 (Sum of equivalent sequences is equivalent).
declarations.statement:
theorem Sequence.add_equiv {a b a' b':ℕ → ℚ} (haa': Equiv a a')
  (hbb': Equiv b b') :

declarations.name: Chapter5.Real.upperBound_def
declarations.doc: Definition 5.5.1 (upper bounds). Here we use the {name}`upperBounds` set defined in Mathlib.
declarations.statement: theorem Real.upperBound_def (E: Set Real) (M: Real) : M ∈ upperBounds E ↔ ∀ x ∈ E, x ≤ M
example (M: Real) : M ∈ upperBounds (.Icc 0 1) ↔ M ≥ 1
example : ¬ ∃ M : Real, M ∈ upperBounds (.Ioi 0)
example : ∀ M, M ∈ upperBounds (∅ : Set Real)

declarations.name: Chapter5.Real.isLUB_def
declarations.doc: Definition 5.5.5 (least upper bound).  Here we use the {name}`IsLUB` predicate defined in Mathlib.
declarations.statement:
theorem Real.isLUB_def (E: Set Real) (M: Real) :
    IsLUB E M ↔ M ∈ upperBounds E ∧ ∀ M' ∈ upperBounds E, M' ≥ M
example : IsLUB (.Icc 0 1) (1 : Real)
example : ¬∃ M, IsLUB (∅: Set Real) M

declarations.name: Chapter5.Real.LUB_unique
declarations.statement: theorem Real.LUB_unique {E: Set Real} {M M': Real} (h1: IsLUB E M) (h2: IsLUB E M') : M = M'

declarations.statement:

  (hK: K*((1/(n+1):ℚ):Real) ∈ upperBounds E) (hL: L*((1/(n+1):ℚ):Real) ∉ upperBounds E) :
    ∃ m, L < m
    ∧ m ≤ K
    ∧ m*((1/(n+1):ℚ):Real) ∈ upperBounds E
    ∧ (m-1)*((1/(n+1):ℚ):Real) ∉ upperBounds E

declarations.statement:
theorem Real.upperBound_discrete_unique {E: Set Real} {n:ℕ} {m m':ℤ}

  (hm'1: (((m':ℚ) / (n+1):ℚ):Real) ∈ upperBounds E)
  (hm'2: (((m':ℚ) / (n+1) - 1 / (n+1):ℚ):Real) ∉ upperBounds E) :
    m = m'

sections.title: Chapter 5 epilogue: Isomorphism with the Mathlib real numbers
sections.doc:
In this (technical) epilogue, we show that the "Chapter 5" real numbers {name}`Chapter5.Real` are
isomorphic in various standard senses to the standard real numbers {lean}`ℝ`.  This we do by matching
both structures with Dedekind cuts of the (Mathlib) rational numbers {lean}`ℚ`.

From this point onwards, {name}`Chapter5.Real` will be deprecated, and we will use the standard real
numbers {lean}`ℝ` instead.  In particular, one should use the full Mathlib API for {lean}`ℝ` for all
subsequent chapters, in lieu of the {name}`Chapter5.Real` API.

Filling the {syntax term}`sorry`s here requires both the {name}`Chapter5.Real` API and the Mathlib API for the standard
real numbers {lean}`ℝ`.  As such, they are excellent exercises to prepare you for the aforementioned
transition.

## Tips from past users

Users of the companion who have completed the exercises in this section are welcome to send their tips for future users in this section as PRs.

- (Add tip here)

sections.title: Section 6.1: Convergence and limit laws
sections.doc:
I have attempted to make the translation as faithful a paraphrasing as possible of the original
text. When there is a choice between a more idiomatic Lean solution and a more faithful
translation, I have generally chosen the latter. In particular, there will be places where the
Lean code could be "golfed" to be more elegant and idiomatic, but I have consciously avoided
doing so.

Main constructions and results of this section:

- Definition of $`ε`-closeness, $`ε`-steadiness, and their eventual counterparts.
- Notion of a Cauchy sequence, convergent sequence, and bounded sequence of reals.

declarations.name: Real.close_def
declarations.doc:
Definition 6.1.2 (ε-close). This is similar to the previous notion of ε-closeness, but where
all quantities are real instead of rational.
declarations.statement: theorem Real.close_def (ε x y : ℝ) : ε.Close x y ↔ dist x y ≤ ε

declarations.name: Chapter6.Sequence
declarations.doc:
Definition 6.1.3 (Sequence). This is similar to the Chapter 5 sequence, except that now the
sequence is real-valued. As with Chapter 5, we start sequences from 0 by default.
declarations.statement: structure Sequence

declarations.name: Real.Steady
declarations.statement: abbrev Real.Steady (ε: ℝ) (a: Chapter6.Sequence) : Prop

declarations.name: Real.steady_def
declarations.statement:
lemma Real.steady_def (ε: ℝ) (a: Chapter6.Sequence) :
  ε.Steady a ↔ ∀ n ≥ a.m, ∀ m ≥ a.m, ε.Close (a n) (a m)

declarations.name: Real.EventuallySteady
declarations.statement: abbrev Real.EventuallySteady (ε: ℝ) (a: Chapter6.Sequence) : Prop

declarations.name: Real.eventuallySteady_def
declarations.statement:
lemma Real.eventuallySteady_def (ε: ℝ) (a: Chapter6.Sequence) :
  ε.EventuallySteady a ↔ ∃ N, (N ≥ a.m) ∧ ε.Steady (a.from N)

declarations.name: Chapter6.Sequence.IsCauchy
declarations.statement: abbrev Sequence.IsCauchy (a:Sequence) : Prop

declarations.name: Chapter6.Sequence.isCauchy_def
declarations.statement:
lemma Sequence.isCauchy_def (a:Sequence) :
  a.IsCauchy ↔ ∀ ε > (0:ℝ), ε.EventuallySteady a

declarations.name: Chapter6.Sequence.isCauchy_of_rat
declarations.statement: theorem Sequence.isCauchy_of_rat (a: Chapter5.Sequence) : a.IsCauchy ↔ (a:Sequence).IsCauchy

declarations.name: Real.CloseSeq
declarations.statement: abbrev Real.CloseSeq (ε: ℝ) (a: Chapter6.Sequence) (L:ℝ) : Prop

declarations.name: Real.closeSeq_def
declarations.statement:
theorem Real.closeSeq_def (ε: ℝ) (a: Chapter6.Sequence) (L:ℝ) :
  ε.CloseSeq a L ↔ ∀ n ≥ a.m, dist (a n) L ≤ ε

declarations.name: Real.EventuallyClose
declarations.statement: abbrev Real.EventuallyClose (ε: ℝ) (a: Chapter6.Sequence) (L:ℝ) : Prop

declarations.name: Real.eventuallyClose_def
declarations.statement:
theorem Real.eventuallyClose_def (ε: ℝ) (a: Chapter6.Sequence) (L:ℝ) :
  ε.EventuallyClose a L ↔ ∃ N, (N ≥ a.m) ∧ ε.CloseSeq (a.from N) L

declarations.name: Chapter6.Sequence.tendsTo_iff
declarations.statement:
theorem Sequence.tendsTo_iff (a:Sequence) (L:ℝ) :
  a.TendsTo L ↔ ∀ ε > 0, ∃ N, ∀ n ≥ N, |a n - L| ≤ ε
example : (0.1:ℝ).CloseSeq seq_6_1_6 1
example : ¬ (0.01:ℝ).CloseSeq seq_6_1_6 1
example : (0.01:ℝ).EventuallyClose seq_6_1_6 1
example : seq_6_1_6.TendsTo 1

declarations.name: Chapter6.Sequence.tendsTo_unique
declarations.statement:
theorem Sequence.tendsTo_unique (a:Sequence) {L L':ℝ} (h:L ≠ L') :
    ¬ (a.TendsTo L ∧ a.TendsTo L')

declarations.name: Chapter6.Sequence.Convergent
declarations.statement: abbrev Sequence.Convergent (a:Sequence) : Prop

declarations.name: Chapter6.Sequence.convergent_def
declarations.statement: theorem Sequence.convergent_def (a:Sequence) : a.Convergent ↔ ∃ L, a.TendsTo L

declarations.name: Chapter6.Sequence.Divergent
declarations.statement: abbrev Sequence.Divergent (a:Sequence) : Prop

declarations.name: Chapter6.Sequence.divergent_def
declarations.statement: theorem Sequence.divergent_def (a:Sequence) : a.Divergent ↔ ¬ a.Convergent

declarations.name: Chapter6.lim
declarations.doc: Definition 6.1.8.  We give the limit of a sequence the junk value of {lean}`0` if it is not convergent.
declarations.statement: noncomputable abbrev lim (a:Sequence) : ℝ

declarations.name: Chapter6.Sequence.lim_def
declarations.statement: theorem Sequence.lim_def {a:Sequence} (h: a.Convergent) : a.TendsTo (lim a)

declarations.name: Chapter6.Sequence.lim_eq
declarations.statement:
theorem Sequence.lim_eq {a:Sequence} {L:ℝ} :
a.TendsTo L ↔ a.Convergent ∧ lim a = L

declarations.name: Chapter6.Sequence.lim_harmonic
declarations.statement:
theorem Sequence.lim_harmonic :
    ((fun (n:ℕ) ↦ (n+1:ℝ)⁻¹):Sequence).Convergent ∧ lim ((fun (n:ℕ) ↦ (n+1:ℝ)⁻¹):Sequence) = 0

declarations.name: Chapter6.Sequence.IsCauchy.convergent
declarations.statement: theorem Sequence.IsCauchy.convergent {a:Sequence} (h:a.Convergent) : a.IsCauchy
example : ¬ (0.1:ℝ).EventuallySteady ((fun n ↦ (-1:ℝ)^n):Sequence)
example : ¬ ((fun n ↦ (-1:ℝ)^n):Sequence).IsCauchy
example : ¬ ((fun n ↦ (-1:ℝ)^n):Sequence).Convergent

declarations.name: Chapter6.Sequence.lim_eq_LIM
declarations.doc: Proposition 6.1.15 / Exercise 6.1.6 (Formal limits are genuine limits)
declarations.statement:
theorem Sequence.lim_eq_LIM {a:ℕ → ℚ} (h: (a:Chapter5.Sequence).IsCauchy) :
    ((a:Chapter5.Sequence):Sequence).TendsTo (Chapter5.Real.equivR (Chapter5.LIM a))

declarations.name: Chapter6.Sequence.BoundedBy
declarations.statement: abbrev Sequence.BoundedBy (a:Sequence) (M:ℝ) : Prop

declarations.name: Chapter6.Sequence.boundedBy_def
declarations.statement:
lemma Sequence.boundedBy_def (a:Sequence) (M:ℝ) :
  a.BoundedBy M ↔ ∀ n, |a n| ≤ M

declarations.name: Chapter6.Sequence.IsBounded
declarations.statement: abbrev Sequence.IsBounded (a:Sequence) : Prop

declarations.name: Chapter6.Sequence.isBounded_def
declarations.statement:
lemma Sequence.isBounded_def (a:Sequence) :
  a.IsBounded ↔ ∃ M ≥ 0, a.BoundedBy M

declarations.name: Chapter6.Sequence.bounded_of_convergent
declarations.statement: theorem Sequence.bounded_of_convergent {a:Sequence} (h: a.Convergent) : a.IsBounded
example : ¬ ((fun (n:ℕ) ↦ (n+1:ℝ)):Sequence).IsBounded
example : ¬ ((fun (n:ℕ) ↦ (n+1:ℝ)):Sequence).Convergent

declarations.name: Chapter6.Sequence.tendsTo_add
declarations.doc:
Theorem 6.1.19(a) (limit laws).  The {name}`Sequence.TendsTo` version is more usable than the {name}`lim` version
in applications.
declarations.statement:
theorem Sequence.tendsTo_add {a b:Sequence} {L M:ℝ} (ha: a.TendsTo L) (hb: b.TendsTo M) :
  (a+b).TendsTo (L+M)

declarations.name: Chapter6.Sequence.tendsTo_mul
declarations.doc:
Theorem 6.1.19(b) (limit laws).  The {name}`Sequence.TendsTo` version is more usable than the {name}`lim` version
in applications.
declarations.statement:
theorem Sequence.tendsTo_mul {a b:Sequence} {L M:ℝ} (ha: a.TendsTo L) (hb: b.TendsTo M) :
    (a * b).TendsTo (L * M)

declarations.name: Chapter6.Sequence.tendsTo_smul
declarations.doc:
Theorem 6.1.19(c) (limit laws).  The {name}`Sequence.TendsTo` version is more usable than the {name}`lim` version
in applications.
declarations.statement:
theorem Sequence.tendsTo_smul (c:ℝ) {a:Sequence} {L:ℝ} (ha: a.TendsTo L) :
    (c • a).TendsTo (c * L)

declarations.name: Chapter6.Sequence.tendsTo_sub
declarations.doc:
Theorem 6.1.19(d) (limit laws).  The {name}`Sequence.TendsTo` version is more usable than the {name}`lim` version
in applications.
declarations.statement:
theorem Sequence.tendsTo_sub {a b:Sequence} {L M:ℝ} (ha: a.TendsTo L) (hb: b.TendsTo M) :
    (a - b).TendsTo (L - M)

declarations.name: Chapter6.Sequence.tendsTo_inv
declarations.doc:
Theorem 6.1.19(e) (limit laws).  The {name}`Sequence.TendsTo` version is more usable than the {name}`lim` version
in applications.
declarations.statement:
theorem Sequence.tendsTo_inv {a:Sequence} {L:ℝ} (ha: a.TendsTo L) (hnon: L ≠ 0) :
    (a⁻¹).TendsTo (L⁻¹)

declarations.name: Chapter6.Sequence.tendsTo_div
declarations.doc:
Theorem 6.1.19(f) (limit laws).  The {name}`Sequence.TendsTo` version is more usable than the {name}`lim` version
in applications.
declarations.statement:
theorem Sequence.tendsTo_div {a b:Sequence} {L M:ℝ} (ha: a.TendsTo L) (hb: b.TendsTo M) (hnon: M ≠ 0) :
    (a / b).TendsTo (L / M)

declarations.name: Chapter6.Sequence.tendsTo_max
declarations.doc:
Theorem 6.1.19(g) (limit laws).  The {name}`Sequence.TendsTo` version is more usable than the {name}`lim` version
in applications.
declarations.statement:
theorem Sequence.tendsTo_max {a b:Sequence} {L M:ℝ} (ha: a.TendsTo L) (hb: b.TendsTo M) :
    (max a b).TendsTo (max L M)

declarations.name: Chapter6.Sequence.tendsTo_min
declarations.statement:
theorem Sequence.tendsTo_min {a b:Sequence} {L M:ℝ} (ha: a.TendsTo L) (hb: b.TendsTo M) :
    (min a b).TendsTo (min L M)

declarations.name: Chapter6.Sequence.mono_if
declarations.statement: theorem Sequence.mono_if {a: ℕ → ℝ} (ha: ∀ n, a (n+1) > a n) {n m:ℕ} (hnm: m > n) : a m > a n

declarations.name: Chapter6.Sequence.tendsTo_of_from
declarations.statement:
theorem Sequence.tendsTo_of_from {a: Sequence} {c:ℝ} (m:ℤ) :
    a.TendsTo c ↔ (a.from m).TendsTo c

declarations.name: Chapter6.Sequence.tendsTo_of_shift
declarations.statement:
theorem Sequence.tendsTo_of_shift {a: Sequence} {c:ℝ} (k:ℕ) :
    a.TendsTo c ↔ (Sequence.mk' a.m (fun n : {n // n ≥ a.m} ↦ a (n+k))).TendsTo c

declarations.name: Chapter6.Sequence.isBounded_of_rat
declarations.statement:
theorem Sequence.isBounded_of_rat (a: Chapter5.Sequence) :
    a.IsBounded ↔ (a:Sequence).IsBounded

declarations.name: Chapter6.Sequence.lim_div_fail
declarations.statement:
theorem Sequence.lim_div_fail :
    ∃ a b, a.Convergent
    ∧ b.Convergent
    ∧ lim b = 0
    ∧ ¬ ((a / b).Convergent ∧ lim (a / b) = lim a / lim b)

declarations.name: Chapter6.Chapter5.Sequence.equiv_rat
declarations.statement:
theorem Chapter5.Sequence.equiv_rat (a b: ℕ → ℚ) :
  Chapter5.Sequence.Equiv a b ↔ Chapter5.Sequence.RatEquiv a b

sections.title: Section 6.2: The extended real number system
sections.doc:
I have attempted to make the translation as faithful a paraphrasing as possible of the original
text. When there is a choice between a more idiomatic Lean solution and a more faithful
translation, I have generally chosen the latter. In particular, there will be places where the
Lean code could be "golfed" to be more elegant and idiomatic, but I have consciously avoided
doing so.

Main constructions and results of this section:

- Some API for Mathlib's extended reals {name}`EReal`, particularly with regard to the supremum
  operation {name}`sSup` and infimum operation {name}`sInf`.

declarations.name: EReal.def
declarations.statement: theorem EReal.def (x:EReal) : (∃ (y:Real), y = x) ∨ x = ⊤ ∨ x = ⊥

declarations.name: EReal.neg_of_real
declarations.statement: theorem EReal.neg_of_real (x:Real) : -(x:EReal) = (-x:ℝ)

declarations.name: EReal.le_iff
declarations.statement:
theorem EReal.le_iff (x y:EReal) :
    x ≤ y ↔ (∃ (x' y':Real), x = x' ∧ y = y' ∧ x' ≤ y') ∨ y = ⊤ ∨ x = ⊥

declarations.name: EReal.lt_iff
declarations.statement: theorem EReal.lt_iff (x y:EReal) : x < y ↔ x ≤ y ∧ x ≠ y
example : (3:EReal) ≤ (5:EReal)
example : (3:EReal) < ⊤
example : (⊥:EReal) < ⊤
example : ¬ (3:EReal) ≤ ⊥

declarations.name: EReal.refl
declarations.statement: theorem EReal.refl (x:EReal) : x ≤ x

declarations.name: EReal.trichotomy
declarations.statement: theorem EReal.trichotomy (x y:EReal) : x < y ∨ x = y ∨ x > y

declarations.name: EReal.not_lt_and_eq
declarations.statement: theorem EReal.not_lt_and_eq (x y:EReal) : ¬ (x < y ∧ x = y)

declarations.name: EReal.not_gt_and_eq
declarations.statement: theorem EReal.not_gt_and_eq (x y:EReal) : ¬ (x > y ∧ x = y)

declarations.name: EReal.not_lt_and_gt
declarations.statement: theorem EReal.not_lt_and_gt (x y:EReal) : ¬ (x < y ∧ x > y)

declarations.name: EReal.trans
declarations.statement: theorem EReal.trans {x y z:EReal} (hxy : x ≤ y) (hyz: y ≤ z) : x ≤ z

declarations.name: EReal.neg_of_lt
declarations.statement: theorem EReal.neg_of_lt {x y:EReal} (hxy : x ≤ y): -y ≤ -x

declarations.name: EReal.sup_of_bounded_nonempty
declarations.statement:
theorem EReal.sup_of_bounded_nonempty {E: Set ℝ} (hbound: BddAbove E) (hnon: E.Nonempty) :
    sSup ((fun (x:ℝ) ↦ (x:EReal)) '' E) = sSup E

declarations.name: EReal.sup_of_unbounded_nonempty
declarations.statement:
theorem EReal.sup_of_unbounded_nonempty {E: Set ℝ} (hunbound: ¬ BddAbove E) (hnon: E.Nonempty) :
    sSup ((fun (x:ℝ) ↦ (x:EReal)) '' E) = ⊤

declarations.name: EReal.sup_of_empty
declarations.statement: theorem EReal.sup_of_empty : sSup (∅:Set EReal) = ⊥

declarations.name: EReal.sup_of_infty_mem
declarations.statement: theorem EReal.sup_of_infty_mem {E: Set EReal} (hE: ⊤ ∈ E) : sSup E = ⊤

declarations.name: EReal.sup_of_neg_infty_mem
declarations.statement: theorem EReal.sup_of_neg_infty_mem {E: Set EReal} : sSup E = sSup (E \ {⊥})

declarations.name: Example_6_2_7
declarations.statement: abbrev Example_6_2_7 : Set EReal

declarations.name: Example_6_2_8
declarations.statement: abbrev Example_6_2_8 : Set EReal

declarations.name: Example_6_2_9
declarations.statement: abbrev Example_6_2_9 : Set EReal

declarations.name: EReal.mem_le_sup
declarations.statement: theorem EReal.mem_le_sup (E: Set EReal) {x:EReal} (hx: x ∈ E) : x ≤ sSup E

declarations.name: EReal.mem_ge_inf
declarations.statement: theorem EReal.mem_ge_inf (E: Set EReal) {x:EReal} (hx: x ∈ E) : sInf E ≤ x

declarations.name: EReal.sup_le_upper
declarations.statement: theorem EReal.sup_le_upper (E: Set EReal) {M:EReal} (hM: M ∈ upperBounds E) : sSup E ≤ M

declarations.name: EReal.inf_ge_lower
declarations.statement: theorem EReal.inf_ge_lower (E: Set EReal) {M:EReal} (hM: M ∈ lowerBounds E) : sInf E ≥ M

sections.title: Section 6.3: Suprema and infima of sequences
sections.doc:
I have attempted to make the translation as faithful a paraphrasing as possible of the original
text. When there is a choice between a more idiomatic Lean solution and a more faithful
translation, I have generally chosen the latter. In particular, there will be places where the
Lean code could be "golfed" to be more elegant and idiomatic, but I have consciously avoided
doing so.

Main constructions and results of this section:

- Suprema and infima of sequences.

declarations.name: Chapter6.Sequence.sup
declarations.statement: noncomputable abbrev Sequence.sup (a:Sequence) : EReal

declarations.name: Chapter6.Sequence.inf
declarations.statement: noncomputable abbrev Sequence.inf (a:Sequence) : EReal
example : ((fun (n:ℕ) ↦ (-1:ℝ)^(n+1)):Sequence).sup = 1
example : ((fun (n:ℕ) ↦ (-1:ℝ)^(n+1)):Sequence).inf = -1
example : ((fun (n:ℕ) ↦ 1/((n:ℝ)+1)):Sequence).sup = 1
example : ((fun (n:ℕ) ↦ 1/((n:ℝ)+1)):Sequence).inf = 0
example : ((fun (n:ℕ) ↦ (n+1:ℝ)):Sequence).sup = ⊤
example : ((fun (n:ℕ) ↦ (n+1:ℝ)):Sequence).inf = 1

declarations.name: Chapter6.Sequence.le_sup
declarations.statement: theorem Sequence.le_sup {a:Sequence} {n:ℤ} (hn: n ≥ a.m) : a n ≤ a.sup

declarations.name: Chapter6.Sequence.sup_le_upper
declarations.statement: theorem Sequence.sup_le_upper {a:Sequence} {M:EReal} (h: ∀ n ≥ a.m, a n ≤ M) : a.sup ≤ M

declarations.name: Chapter6.Sequence.exists_between_lt_sup
declarations.statement:
theorem Sequence.exists_between_lt_sup {a:Sequence} {y:EReal} (h: y < a.sup ) :
    ∃ n ≥ a.m, y < a n ∧ a n ≤ a.sup

declarations.name: Chapter6.Sequence.ge_inf
declarations.statement: theorem Sequence.ge_inf {a:Sequence} {n:ℤ} (hn: n ≥ a.m) : a n ≥ a.inf

declarations.name: Chapter6.Sequence.inf_ge_lower
declarations.statement: theorem Sequence.inf_ge_lower {a:Sequence} {M:EReal} (h: ∀ n ≥ a.m, a n ≥ M) : a.inf ≥ M

declarations.name: Chapter6.Sequence.exists_between_gt_inf
declarations.statement:
theorem Sequence.exists_between_gt_inf {a:Sequence} {y:EReal} (h: y > a.inf ) :
    ∃ n ≥ a.m, y > a n ∧ a n ≥ a.inf

declarations.name: Chapter6.Sequence.convergent_of_monotone
declarations.statement:
theorem Sequence.convergent_of_monotone {a:Sequence} (hbound: a.BddAbove) (hmono: a.IsMonotone) :
    a.Convergent

declarations.name: Chapter6.Sequence.lim_of_monotone
declarations.statement:
theorem Sequence.lim_of_monotone {a:Sequence} (hbound: a.BddAbove) (hmono: a.IsMonotone) :
    lim a = a.sup

declarations.name: Chapter6.Example_6_3_9
declarations.statement: noncomputable abbrev Example_6_3_9 (n:ℕ)
example : (Example_6_3_9:Sequence).IsMonotone
example : (Example_6_3_9:Sequence).BddAboveBy 4
example : (Example_6_3_9:Sequence).Convergent
example : lim (Example_6_3_9:Sequence) ≤ 4

declarations.name: Chapter6.lim_of_exp
declarations.statement:
theorem lim_of_exp {x:ℝ} (hpos: 0 < x) (hbound: x < 1) :

sections.title: Section 6.7: Real exponentiation, part II
sections.doc:
I have attempted to make the translation as faithful a paraphrasing as possible of the original
text. When there is a choice between a more idiomatic Lean solution and a more faithful
translation, I have generally chosen the latter. In particular, there will be places where the
Lean code could be "golfed" to be more elegant and idiomatic, but I have consciously avoided
doing so.

Main constructions and results of this section:

- Real exponentiation.

Because the Chapter 5 reals have been deprecated in favor of the Mathlib reals, and Mathlib real
exponentiation is defined without first going through rational exponentiation, we will adopt a
somewhat awkward compromise, in that we will initially accept the Mathlib exponentiation operation
(with all its API) when the exponent is a rational, and use this to define a notion of real
exponentiation which in the epilogue to this chapter we will show is identical to the Mathlib operation.

sections.title: Chapter 6 epilogue: Connections with Mathlib limits
sections.doc:
In this (technical) epilogue, we show that various operations and properties we have defined for
"Chapter 6" sequences {name}`Chapter6.Sequence` are equivalent to Mathlib operations.  Note however
that Mathlib's operations are defined in far greater generality than the setting of real-valued
sequences, in particular using the language of filters.

sections.doc:

translation, I have generally chosen the latter. In particular, there will be places where the
Lean code could be "golfed" to be more elegant and idiomatic, but I have consciously avoided

Technical note: it is convenient in Lean to extend finite sequences (usually by zero) to be
functions on the entire integers.

Main constructions and results of this section:

declarations.name: Finset.sum_of_empty
declarations.statement: theorem sum_of_empty {n m:ℤ} (h: n < m) (a: ℤ → ℝ) : ∑ i ∈ Icc m n, a i = 0

declarations.name: Finset.sum_of_nonempty
declarations.doc:
Definition 7.1.1. This is similar to Mathlib's {name}`Finset.sum_Icc_succ_top` except that the
latter involves summation over the natural numbers rather than integers.
declarations.statement:
theorem sum_of_nonempty {n m:ℤ} (h: n ≥ m-1) (a: ℤ → ℝ) :
    ∑ i ∈ Icc m (n+1), a i = ∑ i ∈ Icc m n, a i + a (n+1)
example (a: ℤ → ℝ) (m n:ℤ) : ∑ i ∈ Icc m n, a i = ∑ j ∈ Icc m n, a j

  ∑ i ∈ Icc m n, a i + ∑ i ∈ Icc (n+1) p, a i = ∑ i ∈ Icc m p, a i

  (f: X' → ℝ) (g h: Icc (1:ℤ) n → X) (hg: Function.Bijective g) (hh: Function.Bijective h) :
    ∑ i ∈ Icc (1:ℤ) n, (if hi:i ∈ Icc (1:ℤ) n then f (g ⟨ i, hi ⟩) else 0)
    = ∑ i ∈ Icc (1:ℤ) n, (if hi: i ∈ Icc (1:ℤ) n then f (h ⟨ i, hi ⟩) else 0)

    ∑ i ∈ X, f i = ∑ i ∈ Icc (1:ℤ) n, (if hi:i ∈ Icc (1:ℤ) n then f (g ⟨ i, hi ⟩) else 0)
